name: Pressure (P = F/A)
description: Computes pressure as force÷area, the force distributed per unit area, in pascals from force in newtons and area in m².
notes: Force must act perpendicular to the surface. Area must be nonzero; 1 pascal equals 1 N/m², so use m² to get pascals.

name: Density (ρ = m/V)
description: Computes the density of a substance as its mass m divided by its volume v. The result is the mass per unit volume in kilograms per cubic metre.
notes: Mass in kilograms and volume in cubic metres give kg/m³; for reference, water is about 1000 kg/m³. Assumes the material is uniform throughout.

name: Hydrostatic Pressure (ρgh)
description: Gives the gauge pressure exerted by a static column of fluid of density rho at depth h, in a gravitational field g. The pressure increases linearly with depth and does not depend on the shape or width of the container.
notes: This is the pressure due to the fluid alone; add surface (atmospheric) pressure to get absolute pressure. Keep density in kg/m³ and depth in meters.

name: Absolute Pressure at Depth
description: Computes the absolute pressure at depth h in a fluid by adding the hydrostatic pressure of the fluid column (rho g h) to the pressure P0 acting on the surface. Both the fluid weight and the overlying surface pressure contribute.
notes: P0 is often atmospheric pressure (about 101325 Pa). Use SI units throughout; the result is absolute pressure, not gauge pressure.

name: Buoyant Force (Archimedes)
description: Calculates the upward buoyant force on a submerged or floating object by Archimedes' principle, equal to the weight of the fluid displaced. It depends on the fluid density, gravity, and the displaced volume, not on the object's own material.
notes: V is the volume of fluid displaced, which for a fully submerged body equals its own volume. Use fluid density, not the object's density, in kg/m³.

name: Bernoulli Total Pressure
description: Sums the three terms of Bernoulli's equation — static pressure, dynamic pressure (half rho v squared), and hydrostatic pressure (rho g h) — to give the total pressure along a streamline. For ideal steady flow this total stays constant along the streamline.
notes: Valid for incompressible, non-viscous, steady flow along a single streamline. All terms must share consistent SI units; h is the height relative to a chosen reference level.

name: Volumetric Flow Rate (Q = A·v)
description: Computes the volumetric flow rate through a cross-section as the product of the cross-sectional area A and the average flow velocity v. It represents the volume of fluid passing the section each second.
notes: Assumes velocity is uniform across the section (or v is the mean velocity). Keep area in m² and velocity in m/s to obtain m³/s.

name: Mass Flow Rate
description: Gives the mass flow rate through a cross-section as the product of fluid density, cross-sectional area, and flow velocity. It is the mass of fluid crossing the section per second, equal to density times the volumetric flow rate.
notes: Assumes uniform density and velocity across the section. Use SI units (kg/m³, m², m/s) to get kilograms per second.

name: Continuity Equation (solve for v2)
description: Uses the continuity equation for incompressible flow to find the outlet velocity from the inlet area, inlet velocity, and outlet area. Because the volume flow rate is conserved, a narrower outlet forces a faster flow.
notes: Valid only for incompressible, steady flow where mass is conserved. Both areas must use the same unit; a smaller outlet area A2 gives a larger v2.

name: Reynolds Number
description: Computes the Reynolds number, a dimensionless ratio of inertial to viscous forces in a flow, from density, velocity, a characteristic length, and dynamic viscosity. It predicts whether flow tends to be laminar or turbulent.
notes: Roughly, pipe flow is laminar below about 2300 and turbulent above about 4000. The characteristic length depends on geometry (e.g. pipe diameter); the result is dimensionless.

name: Pascal's Principle (Pressure = F/A)
description: Gives the pressure produced by a force F applied over an area A, the basic definition of pressure underlying Pascal's principle. The same pressure is transmitted undiminished throughout a confined fluid.
notes: Force in newtons and area in m² give pressure in pascals. Pressure and force are distinct: a small force on a tiny area can yield very high pressure.

name: Hydraulic Press Output Force
description: Calculates the output force of a hydraulic press by multiplying the input force by the ratio of the output to input piston areas. Because pressure is transmitted equally, a larger output piston multiplies the force accordingly.
notes: Both piston areas must use the same unit. Force is multiplied but the output piston moves a proportionally shorter distance, so work (energy) is not increased.

name: Drag Force
description: Gives the aerodynamic or hydrodynamic drag force on a body moving through a fluid, as one half times fluid density times velocity squared times drag coefficient times reference area. The force in newtons acts opposite to the direction of motion.
notes: Force grows with the square of velocity, so doubling speed quadruples drag. The drag coefficient and reference area must be defined consistently for the same body and Reynolds-number regime.

name: Lift Force
description: Calculates the lift force generated by a wing or lifting surface moving through a fluid, as one half times fluid density times velocity squared times lift coefficient times wing area. The result in newtons acts perpendicular to the flow direction.
notes: The lift coefficient depends on angle of attack and airfoil shape and is not constant. Lift scales with velocity squared, and this form assumes incompressible, attached flow below stall.

name: Stokes Drag
description: Computes the viscous drag force on a small sphere moving slowly through a fluid, as six times pi times dynamic viscosity times sphere radius times velocity. The result in newtons is proportional to speed, unlike high-speed quadratic drag.
notes: Valid only in the creeping-flow regime at very low Reynolds number (roughly below 1) for a rigid sphere. At higher speeds inertial effects dominate and this underestimates the drag.

name: Poiseuille Flow Rate
description: Gives the volumetric flow rate of a viscous fluid through a circular pipe under laminar conditions, as pi times radius to the fourth power times pressure difference divided by eight times viscosity times length. The result is in cubic meters per second.
notes: Flow depends on the fourth power of radius, so small diameter changes have large effects. Valid only for steady, laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian fluid; turbulence breaks this relation.

name: Froude Number
description: Computes the dimensionless Froude number, the ratio of flow inertia to gravity, as velocity divided by the square root of gravity times a characteristic length. Values below 1 indicate subcritical flow and above 1 supercritical flow.
notes: The characteristic length is typically flow depth for open channels. Use the correct length scale for your problem, since the threshold at Fr equals 1 marks the critical-flow transition.

name: Mach Number
description: Gives the Mach number, the dimensionless ratio of an object's speed to the local speed of sound, as velocity divided by sound speed. Values below 1 are subsonic, near 1 transonic, and above 1 supersonic.
notes: The speed of sound depends on the medium and its temperature, so use the local value, not a fixed constant. Compressibility effects become important as the ratio approaches 1.

name: Dynamic Pressure
description: Calculates the dynamic pressure of a moving fluid, the kinetic-energy contribution to Bernoulli's equation, as one half times fluid density times velocity squared. The result in pascals represents the pressure rise when the flow is brought to rest.
notes: This is not the static or total pressure but the velocity-related part. It assumes incompressible flow, so it loses accuracy at high Mach numbers where density changes matter.

name: Torricelli Velocity
description: Gives the ideal efflux velocity of a fluid jet leaving an opening under a head of height h, as the square root of two times gravity times head. The result in meters per second equals the speed a body would reach falling freely through the same height.
notes: Assumes an ideal, frictionless fluid and neglects viscosity and contraction of the jet. Real discharge is lower, which is accounted for with a discharge coefficient.

name: Darcy-Weisbach Pressure Drop
description: Computes the frictional pressure drop for fluid flowing through a pipe, as the friction factor times length over diameter times the dynamic pressure (one half density times velocity squared). The result in pascals is the energy loss due to wall friction.
notes: The friction factor depends on Reynolds number and pipe roughness and must be chosen accordingly. Applies to fully developed flow in a uniform pipe; use a separate approach for fittings and bends.

name: Hydraulic Radius
description: Gives the hydraulic radius of a channel or conduit, defined as the flow cross-sectional area divided by the wetted perimeter. The result in meters characterizes the flow geometry and feeds into open-channel and friction formulas.
notes: The wetted perimeter includes only the boundary in contact with the fluid, not the free surface. It differs from a geometric radius; for a full circular pipe it equals one quarter of the diameter.

name: Manning Velocity
description: Estimates the average velocity of open-channel flow using Manning's formula, as one over the roughness coefficient times hydraulic radius to the two-thirds power times the square root of channel slope. The result is in meters per second.
notes: This is the SI form with an implicit coefficient of 1; imperial units require a factor of 1.49. The roughness coefficient n is empirical and slope should be the energy or bed slope for uniform flow.

name: Pump Hydraulic Power
description: Computes the hydraulic (useful) power delivered by a pump to a fluid, as fluid density times gravity times volumetric flow rate times pump head. The result in watts is the rate of energy imparted to the flow.
notes: This is the ideal hydraulic power, not the shaft or electrical input; dividing by pump efficiency gives the actual power required. Head must be the total dynamic head across the pump.

name: Pressure Head
description: Converts a fluid pressure into an equivalent column height, as pressure divided by the product of fluid density and gravity. The result in meters is the height of fluid whose weight produces that pressure.
notes: Uses gauge pressure relative to the local reference; the value depends on the fluid density chosen. It expresses static pressure only, excluding velocity and elevation contributions.

name: Capillary Rise (Jurin's Law)
description: Predicts the height a liquid rises (or falls) in a narrow tube due to surface tension, as two times surface tension times the cosine of the contact angle divided by liquid density, gravity and tube radius. The result is in meters.
notes: The contact angle must be in radians; angles above 90 degrees give a negative result (depression). Assumes a thin cylindrical tube where capillary effects dominate over the liquid weight.

name: Weber Number
description: Gives the dimensionless Weber number, the ratio of fluid inertia to surface tension, as density times velocity squared times a characteristic length divided by surface tension. High values mean inertia dominates, favoring droplet or interface breakup.
notes: Useful in atomization, sprays and multiphase flows to judge droplet stability. The characteristic length must match the relevant scale, such as droplet diameter, for the number to be meaningful.

name: Young-Laplace Capillary Pressure
description: Computes the pressure difference across the curved surface of a spherical droplet or bubble, as two times surface tension divided by radius. The result in pascals is the excess internal pressure caused by surface tension.
notes: This 2*gamma/r form is for a single spherical interface (a droplet); a soap bubble with two surfaces uses 4*gamma/r. Smaller radii produce much larger pressure differences.

name: Newtonian Shear Stress
description: Gives the shear stress in a Newtonian fluid under simple shear, as dynamic viscosity times the velocity difference divided by the gap distance (the velocity gradient). The result in pascals is the tangential stress resisting the shearing.
notes: Valid only for Newtonian fluids where stress is proportional to shear rate, and for a linear velocity profile across the gap. Non-Newtonian fluids need a different constitutive relation.

name: Specific Weight
description: Computes the specific weight (weight per unit volume) of a fluid, as fluid density times gravitational acceleration. The result in newtons per cubic meter is the gravitational force acting on each unit volume of the fluid.
notes: Specific weight depends on local gravity, unlike density, and differs from specific gravity, which is a dimensionless ratio to water. For water it is about 9810 N/m^3.

name: Orifice Discharge
description: Calculates the volumetric flow rate through an orifice under a head h, as the discharge coefficient times orifice area times the square root of two times gravity times head. The result is in cubic meters per second.
notes: The discharge coefficient (typically around 0.6) corrects the ideal Torricelli velocity for jet contraction and friction. Assumes a constant head and free discharge to atmosphere.

name: Venturi Flow Rate
description: Computes the flow rate through a venturi meter from the pressure drop between inlet and throat, as the discharge coefficient times throat area times the square root of two times pressure difference over density and the area-ratio factor. The result is in cubic meters per second.
notes: The factor 1-(a2/a1)^2 accounts for the upstream velocity, so the inlet and throat areas must be entered correctly. Assumes incompressible, steady flow; the discharge coefficient corrects for real losses.

name: Continuity Velocity
description: Gives the average flow velocity from the continuity equation, as volumetric flow rate divided by cross-sectional area. The result in meters per second is the mean speed of fluid passing through the section.
notes: Assumes incompressible flow and uniform velocity across the section, giving the mean rather than the local peak velocity. For a given flow rate, a smaller area means a proportionally higher velocity.

name: Knudsen Number
description: Computes the dimensionless Knudsen number, the ratio of the molecular mean free path to a characteristic length. It gauges how rarefied a gas is: small values indicate continuum flow, large values free-molecular flow.
notes: Continuum assumptions hold below about 0.01; between 0.1 and 10 flow is transitional and needs slip or kinetic models. The characteristic length should reflect the smallest relevant flow dimension.

name: Euler Number
description: Gives the dimensionless Euler number, the ratio of pressure forces to inertial forces, as pressure difference divided by density times velocity squared. It characterizes pressure losses relative to the dynamic pressure of the flow.
notes: Some definitions include a factor of one half or use 2*dp in the numerator, so check the convention when comparing values. The cavitation number is a related pressure-based dimensionless group.

name: Cauchy Number
description: Computes the dimensionless Cauchy number, the ratio of inertial forces to compressibility (elastic) forces, as density times velocity squared divided by the bulk modulus. High values indicate compressibility effects become significant.
notes: The Cauchy number is the square of the Mach number for an ideal gas, so it links directly to compressible-flow behavior. The bulk modulus must correspond to the fluid's elastic stiffness.

name: Strouhal Number
description: Gives the dimensionless Strouhal number describing oscillating flow, as vortex-shedding frequency times a characteristic length divided by flow velocity. It relates the timescale of unsteady vortex shedding to the flow's convective timescale.
notes: For bluff-body vortex shedding it is often near 0.2 over a wide Reynolds-number range. Use the shedding frequency and the body's cross-stream dimension as the characteristic length.

name: Bond Number
description: Computes the dimensionless Bond number (Eotvos number), the ratio of gravitational (buoyancy) forces to surface-tension forces, as density difference times gravity times length squared divided by surface tension. It indicates whether gravity or capillarity dominates.
notes: Values well below 1 mean surface tension dominates (droplets stay spherical); values above 1 mean gravity flattens the interface. Use the density difference between the two phases, not a single density.

name: Capillary Number
description: Gives the dimensionless capillary number, the ratio of viscous forces to surface-tension forces, as dynamic viscosity times velocity divided by surface tension. It governs the balance between viscous drag and capillarity in multiphase flows.
notes: Low values mean surface tension shapes the interface; high values mean viscous forces deform it. Important in coating, porous-media and microfluidic flows where interfaces are thin.

name: Ohnesorge Number
description: Computes the dimensionless Ohnesorge number, relating viscous forces to inertial and surface-tension forces, as dynamic viscosity divided by the square root of density times surface tension times a characteristic length. It characterizes droplet formation and breakup.
notes: It equals the square root of the Weber number divided by the Reynolds number, independent of velocity. The characteristic length is usually the droplet or jet diameter.

name: Darcy-Weisbach Head Loss
description: Computes the head loss due to pipe friction, as the friction factor times length over diameter times velocity squared divided by two times gravity. The result in meters is the energy loss expressed as an equivalent fluid column height.
notes: This is the head form of the Darcy-Weisbach equation; multiply by density times gravity to get pressure drop. The friction factor depends on Reynolds number and relative roughness.

name: Hagen-Poiseuille Pressure Drop
description: Gives the pressure drop for laminar viscous flow through a circular pipe, as eight times viscosity times length times flow rate divided by pi times radius to the fourth power. The result in pascals is the driving pressure needed to sustain the flow.
notes: The fourth-power dependence on radius makes pressure drop extremely sensitive to pipe diameter. Valid only for steady, laminar, fully developed Newtonian flow; it fails in turbulent regimes.

name: Chezy Velocity
description: Estimates the mean velocity of open-channel flow using the Chezy formula, as the Chezy coefficient times the square root of hydraulic radius times channel slope. The result is in meters per second.
notes: The Chezy coefficient is empirical and depends on channel roughness and geometry; it relates to Manning's n. Assumes steady, uniform flow where the bed slope equals the energy slope.

name: Prandtl Number
description: Computes the dimensionless Prandtl number, the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity, as dynamic viscosity times specific heat capacity divided by thermal conductivity. It compares how quickly momentum and heat diffuse in a fluid.
notes: It is a fluid property independent of flow geometry; values near 0.7 are typical for gases and much higher for oils. Low values mean heat diffuses faster than momentum, as in liquid metals.

name: Stokes Drag Coefficient
description: Computes the drag coefficient of a sphere in creeping flow, as 24 divided by the Reynolds number. This dimensionless value gives the very high drag coefficients characteristic of slow, viscous-dominated flow around a sphere.
notes: Valid only at low Reynolds number (roughly below 1) where Stokes' law applies. As Reynolds number rises, the true drag coefficient levels off near 0.4 rather than following this inverse relation.

name: Kinematic Viscosity
description: Converts dynamic viscosity to kinematic viscosity by dividing dynamic viscosity by fluid density. The result in square meters per second represents the fluid's momentum diffusivity, the ratio governing how viscous effects spread.
notes: Kinematic viscosity combines viscosity and density into one property used in Reynolds-number calculations. Both inputs should be at the same temperature since each varies with it.

name: Pitot Tube Velocity
description: Recovers flow velocity from a pitot tube's measured dynamic pressure, as the square root of two times dynamic pressure divided by fluid density. The result in meters per second follows from inverting the dynamic-pressure relation.
notes: The pressure must be the dynamic (total minus static) pressure, and it assumes incompressible flow. At high speeds compressibility corrections are needed for accurate results.

name: Buoyant Force
description: Computes the buoyant force on a submerged or floating body by Archimedes' principle, as fluid density times gravity times displaced volume. The result in newtons equals the weight of the fluid displaced and acts upward.
notes: Use the density of the surrounding fluid and the volume it actually displaces, which for a floating body is only the submerged part. The force is independent of the body's own weight or material.

name: Power Number
description: Gives the dimensionless power number of a stirred-tank impeller, as impeller power divided by fluid density times rotational speed cubed times impeller diameter to the fifth power. It characterizes the power draw of mixing impellers.
notes: Rotational speed must be in revolutions per second (consistent with 1/s), and the strong diameter dependence makes units critical. For a given impeller it is roughly constant in the turbulent regime.

name: Hydraulic Diameter
description: Computes the hydraulic diameter of a non-circular duct, as four times the flow cross-sectional area divided by the wetted perimeter. The result in meters is an equivalent diameter used in Reynolds-number and friction calculations.
notes: It reduces to the actual diameter for a full circular pipe and equals four times the hydraulic radius. The wetted perimeter counts only the boundary in contact with the fluid.

name: Peclet Number
description: Computes the dimensionless Peclet number for heat transport, the ratio of advection to diffusion, as flow velocity times a characteristic length divided by thermal diffusivity. High values mean advection dominates over conduction.
notes: This thermal Peclet number equals the product of Reynolds and Prandtl numbers; a mass-transfer version uses mass diffusivity instead. Choose the length scale relevant to the transport process.

name: Galilei Number
description: Gives the dimensionless Galilei number, the ratio of gravitational forces to viscous forces, as gravity times a characteristic length cubed divided by kinematic viscosity squared. It appears in problems of buoyancy-driven and film flows.
notes: It is essentially the Grashof number without the temperature-driven density term, and depends strongly on the length scale (cubed). Use kinematic, not dynamic, viscosity here.

name: Blasius Friction Factor
description: Computes the Darcy friction factor for smooth-pipe turbulent flow via the Blasius correlation, 0.316*Re^(-0.25), as a function of Reynolds number Re. It gives the dimensionless resistance used in pressure-drop and head-loss calculations.
notes: Valid for hydraulically smooth pipes with Re roughly between 4000 and 1e5. This is the Darcy (not Fanning) factor, which is four times larger than Fanning.

name: Swamee-Jain Friction Factor
description: Computes the Darcy friction factor from the Swamee-Jain equation, an explicit approximation to the Colebrook equation, using relative roughness eps/D and Reynolds number Re. It avoids the iterative Colebrook solution for turbulent pipe flow.
notes: The log is base 10. Valid roughly for eps/D between 1e-6 and 1e-2 and Re between 5000 and 1e8. Approximates Colebrook to within a few percent.

name: Haaland Friction Factor
description: Computes the Darcy friction factor via the Haaland equation, an explicit approximation to Colebrook using relative roughness eps/D and Reynolds number Re. It gives turbulent-flow friction in a single non-iterative expression.
notes: The log is base 10. Applicable to turbulent flow (Re above about 4000). It is typically accurate to within about 2 percent of the implicit Colebrook result.

name: Grashof Number
description: Computes the Grashof number, g*beta*(Ts - Tinf)*L^3/nu^2, the dimensionless ratio of buoyancy to viscous forces in natural convection. It characterizes how strongly a temperature difference drives buoyant flow along a surface of length L.
notes: beta is the thermal expansion coefficient (1/T for an ideal gas). Ts - Tinf is the surface-to-fluid temperature difference. Large Grashof numbers signal transition to turbulent free convection.

name: Rayleigh Number (Natural Convection)
description: Computes the Rayleigh number, g*beta*(Ts - Tinf)*L^3/(nu*alpha), the product of the Grashof and Prandtl numbers governing natural convection. It measures whether heat transfer across a fluid layer is dominated by conduction or by buoyant convection.
notes: Below a critical value (about 1708 for a heated layer) heat moves by conduction; above it convection cells form. alpha is thermal diffusivity, nu kinematic viscosity.

name: Dittus-Boelter Nusselt Number
description: Computes the Nusselt number for turbulent flow in a tube using the Dittus-Boelter correlation, 0.023*Re^0.8*Pr^0.4, from the Reynolds and Prandtl numbers. The Nusselt number gives convective relative to conductive heat transfer for finding the heat transfer coefficient.
notes: The exponent 0.4 on Pr applies to heating of the fluid; use 0.3 for cooling. Valid for Re above about 10000, Pr from 0.6 to 160, and long tubes.

name: Schmidt Number
description: Computes the Schmidt number, nu/Dm, the ratio of momentum diffusivity (kinematic viscosity) to mass diffusivity. It is the mass-transfer analogue of the Prandtl number, describing the relative thickness of velocity and concentration boundary layers.
notes: Dimensionless. For gases it is near 1; for liquids it is much larger (order 100 to 1000) because mass diffuses slowly compared with momentum.

name: Lewis Number
description: Computes the Lewis number, alpha/Dm, the ratio of thermal diffusivity to mass diffusivity. It compares how fast heat spreads versus how fast a species diffuses, and equals the Schmidt number divided by the Prandtl number.
notes: Dimensionless. A Lewis number of 1 means heat and mass diffuse equally fast, a common simplifying assumption in combustion and evaporation analyses.

name: Stanton Number
description: Computes the Stanton number, h/(rho*u*cp), the ratio of heat actually transferred to a fluid to its thermal capacity to carry heat by convection. It is a dimensionless heat-transfer coefficient equal to Nu/(Re*Pr).
notes: h is the convective heat transfer coefficient, u the flow velocity, cp the specific heat. It links directly to the Colburn analogy between heat and momentum transfer.

name: Colburn j-Factor
description: Computes the Colburn j-factor for heat transfer, St*Pr^(2/3), from the Stanton and Prandtl numbers. It recasts the Stanton number into a form that, by the Chilton-Colburn analogy, equals half the friction factor for many flows.
notes: The analogy jH = f/2 lets friction data estimate heat transfer, and jH = jD links heat and mass transfer. Valid for Pr roughly 0.6 to 60.

name: Bulk Richardson Number
description: Computes the bulk Richardson number, g*beta*dT*L/u^2, the ratio of buoyancy (stabilizing or destabilizing) to shear-driven kinetic energy in a stratified flow. It indicates whether turbulence is suppressed or enhanced by temperature stratification.
notes: Positive values (stable stratification) suppress turbulence; below a critical value near 0.25 shear can overcome stability and generate turbulence. dT is the temperature difference over length L.

name: Rossby Number
description: Computes the Rossby number, U/(f*L), the ratio of inertial to Coriolis forces in a rotating flow, from velocity scale U, Coriolis parameter f, and length scale L. It measures how strongly planetary rotation influences the flow.
notes: Small values (much less than 1) mean rotation dominates, as in large-scale ocean and atmospheric flows; large values mean rotation is negligible. f is the Coriolis parameter.

name: Ekman Number
description: Computes the Ekman number, nu/(f*L^2), the ratio of viscous to Coriolis forces in a rotating fluid, from eddy viscosity nu, Coriolis parameter f, and length scale L. It characterizes the thickness of the frictional Ekman boundary layer.
notes: Small Ekman numbers mean rotation dominates viscosity, typical of geophysical flows. nu here is an eddy (turbulent) viscosity, not molecular viscosity.

name: Womersley Number
description: Computes the Womersley number, R*sqrt(omega*rho/mu), a dimensionless measure of pulsatile flow comparing transient inertial to viscous forces in a vessel of radius R oscillating at angular frequency omega. It describes how the velocity profile responds to unsteady, oscillating pressure.
notes: Small values (below about 1) give quasi-steady parabolic profiles; large values give flatter, phase-lagged profiles. Widely used for blood flow in arteries.

name: Dean Number
description: Computes the Dean number, Re*sqrt(D/(2*Rc)), characterizing flow in a curved pipe of diameter D coiled at radius Rc. It quantifies the strength of the secondary swirling (Dean) vortices induced by centrifugal effects in curved channels.
notes: Above a critical Dean number, counter-rotating Dean vortices appear and enhance mixing and pressure drop. D/(2*Rc) is the curvature ratio.

name: Cavitation Number
description: Computes the cavitation number, (p - pv)/(0.5*rho*v^2), the ratio of the margin above vapor pressure to the flow's dynamic pressure. It indicates how likely a flowing liquid is to cavitate, forming vapor bubbles where local pressure drops to vapor pressure.
notes: Lower values mean higher cavitation risk; below a device-specific critical value bubbles form and can cause erosion. pv is the liquid's vapor pressure at its temperature.

name: Pressure Coefficient
description: Computes the pressure coefficient, (p - pinf)/(0.5*rho*vinf^2), the local pressure relative to freestream expressed in units of freestream dynamic pressure. It is the standard dimensionless measure of the pressure field over an aerodynamic body.
notes: Cp = 1 at a stagnation point in incompressible flow; negative values indicate suction (pressure below freestream). pinf and vinf are freestream conditions.

name: Schiller-Naumann Drag Coefficient
description: Computes the drag coefficient of a sphere using the Schiller-Naumann correlation, (24/Re)*(1 + 0.15*Re^0.687), as a function of particle Reynolds number Re. It extends the Stokes law drag into the intermediate Reynolds-number regime.
notes: Valid for spherical particles up to Re of about 1000. At very low Re it reduces to the Stokes result 24/Re; the correction term accounts for inertial effects.

name: Stokes Settling Velocity
description: Computes the terminal settling velocity of a small sphere in the Stokes (creeping-flow) regime, g*d^2*(rhop - rhof)/(18*mu), balancing gravity, buoyancy, and viscous drag. It gives the steady fall speed of a particle of diameter d in a fluid of viscosity mu.
notes: Valid only for very small particle Reynolds numbers (below about 1), i.e. fine particles or viscous fluids. A negative result (rhop < rhof) means the particle rises.

name: Newton-Regime Terminal Velocity
expression: sqrt(4 * g * d * (rhop - rhof) / (3 * Cd * rhof))
description: Computes the terminal settling velocity of a particle in the high-Reynolds Newton regime, sqrt(4*g*d*(rhop - rhof)/(3*Cd*rhof)), where inertial drag with a roughly constant drag coefficient Cd balances net gravity. It applies to large or fast-settling particles.
notes: Cd is roughly constant (about 0.44) for Reynolds numbers between about 1000 and 2e5. Requires rhop greater than rhof for the particle to settle.

name: Shields Parameter
description: Computes the Shields parameter, tauw/((rhos - rho)*g*d), the dimensionless bed shear stress that governs the onset of sediment motion. It compares the fluid's shear stress driving grains to the submerged weight resisting their movement.
notes: Motion begins above a critical Shields value (roughly 0.03 to 0.06 depending on grain Reynolds number). rhos is sediment density, d the grain diameter.

name: Rouse Number
description: Computes the Rouse number, ws/(kappa*ustar), the ratio of a sediment particle's settling velocity to the turbulent upward mixing set by the shear velocity. It classifies whether sediment travels as bed load, suspended load, or wash load.
notes: Large values (above about 2.5) mean bed load; small values (below about 0.8) mean fully suspended wash load. kappa is the von Karman constant, about 0.41.

name: Shear (Friction) Velocity
description: Computes the shear (friction) velocity, sqrt(tauw/rho), a velocity scale formed from the wall shear stress and fluid density. Though not a real flow speed, it sets the scale of near-wall turbulence and appears throughout boundary-layer theory.
notes: tauw is the wall (bed) shear stress. This velocity scale underlies the law of the wall and dimensionless wall units; it is not the actual fluid velocity.

name: Law of the Wall Velocity
description: Computes the mean velocity in a turbulent boundary layer from the logarithmic law of the wall, (ustar/kappa)*ln(y/y0), at distance y from a wall with roughness length y0. It gives the characteristic logarithmic velocity profile of wall-bounded turbulence.
notes: Valid in the logarithmic (overlap) layer, not the viscous sublayer very near the wall. y0 is the height where the profile extrapolates to zero velocity; kappa is about 0.41.

name: Hazen-Williams Head Loss
description: Computes the friction head loss in a water pipe using the empirical Hazen-Williams equation, 10.67*L*Q^1.852/(C^1.852*D^4.87), from length L, flow rate Q, roughness coefficient C, and diameter D. It gives the energy loss commonly used in water-distribution design.
notes: This SI form assumes water near room temperature; the constant is unit-specific. Higher C means smoother pipe. Not valid for other fluids or very cold or hot water.

name: Joukowsky Water Hammer Surge
description: Computes the Joukowsky pressure surge, rho*a*dv, the peak pressure rise from a sudden change in flow velocity dv in a pipe carrying a fluid of density rho with pressure-wave speed a. It gives the classic water-hammer overpressure from instantaneous valve closure.
notes: Assumes the velocity change is faster than the pipe's wave-return time (rapid closure); slower changes give smaller surges. a is the acoustic wave speed in the fluid-pipe system.

name: Korteweg Pipe Wave Speed
description: Computes the speed of a pressure (water-hammer) wave travelling along a liquid-filled elastic pipe. The rigid-pipe sound speed sqrt(K/rho) is reduced by the pipe wall's flexibility, captured by the ratio (K*D)/(Ep*t) of fluid to wall stiffness.
notes: All moduli and pressures must be in pascals and lengths in metres. Thin-wall assumption; a stiffer or thicker wall raises the speed toward the fluid's own sound speed.

name: Borda-Carnot Expansion Loss
description: Gives the head loss caused by a sudden pipe or channel expansion, where the flow decelerates from velocity v1 to v2. The lost energy equals the kinetic energy of the velocity difference, (v1-v2)^2/(2g), expressed as a height of fluid.
notes: Valid for an abrupt (sudden) enlargement, not a gradual diffuser. Velocities are cross-section averages; the result is a head in metres, convert to pressure by multiplying by rho*g.

name: Hydraulic Jump Sequent Depth
description: Uses the momentum equation to find the downstream (sequent) depth after a hydraulic jump in a rectangular channel, given the upstream depth y1 and upstream Froude number Fr. The deeper subcritical flow results from supercritical flow slowing abruptly.
notes: Requires Fr>1 (supercritical inflow) for a real jump; at Fr=1 the depths are equal. Applies to rectangular channels with roughly horizontal bed and negligible friction across the jump.

name: Critical Depth (Rectangular Channel)
description: Returns the critical flow depth in a rectangular open channel, at which specific energy is minimum for the given discharge per unit width q. It is the cube root of q^2/g and marks the boundary between subcritical and supercritical flow.
notes: q is discharge per unit width (m^2/s), not total flow. Valid for rectangular channels only; at this depth the Froude number equals 1.

name: Specific Energy (Open Channel)
description: Computes the specific energy in an open channel, the energy per unit weight measured from the channel bed. It is the sum of the flow depth y and the velocity head q^2/(2*g*y^2), where q is discharge per unit width.
notes: q is per unit width (m^2/s). For a fixed q, specific energy has a minimum at the critical depth; two depths (subcritical and supercritical) can share the same energy.

name: Rectangular Weir Discharge
description: Estimates the volumetric flow over a sharp-crested rectangular weir from the head H measured above the crest. Flow scales with the crest width b and with H raised to the 1.5 power, adjusted by the discharge coefficient Cd.
notes: H is the upstream head above the crest, not the total water depth. Cd (about 0.62) lumps in contraction and viscous effects; assumes free, ventilated overfall.

name: V-Notch Weir Discharge
description: Gives the discharge over a triangular (V-notch) weir from the head H above the notch vertex and the notch angle theta. Flow varies with H^2.5 and with tan(theta/2), making the V-notch sensitive at low flows.
notes: theta is the full notch angle in radians; H is measured from the vertex. The H^2.5 law gives high resolution at small heads but the notch must run with a free, aerated nappe.

name: Sharp-Edged Orifice Discharge
description: Computes the flow rate through a sharp-edged orifice from Torricelli's velocity sqrt(2*g*h) times the orifice area A, corrected by the discharge coefficient Cd. It combines contraction of the jet and velocity loss into one factor.
notes: h is the head above the orifice centre; Cd (about 0.61) already accounts for the vena contracta and friction. Assumes a large upstream reservoir and free discharge.

name: Venturi Meter Flow Rate
description: Determines the volumetric flow through a Venturi meter from the pressure drop p1-p2 between the inlet and throat. It applies Bernoulli and continuity, with the area ratio A2/A1 accounting for the upstream velocity and Cd for real losses.
notes: Pressures in pascals and areas in m^2; p1 must exceed p2. Assumes incompressible flow; the area ratio term requires A2 smaller than A1 to keep the root real.

name: Pitot-Static Tube Velocity
description: Recovers flow speed from a Pitot-static tube using the difference between stagnation pressure p0 and static pressure p. From Bernoulli's equation the velocity equals sqrt(2*(p0-p)/rho), where that difference is the dynamic pressure.
notes: Requires p0>p and the correct fluid density rho. Valid for incompressible flow (low Mach); at high speeds compressibility corrections are needed.

name: Bingham Plastic Shear Stress
description: Gives the shear stress of a Bingham plastic fluid, which flows only after a yield stress tau0 is exceeded. Above yield the stress rises linearly with shear rate gamma at slope mu, so total stress is tau0 + mu*gamma.
notes: Valid only once the material is yielding (stress above tau0); below yield it behaves as a solid and this linear form does not apply. mu is the plastic viscosity, not an ordinary viscosity.

name: Power-Law Fluid Shear Stress
description: Computes the shear stress of a power-law (Ostwald-de Waele) fluid as K*gamma^n. The consistency index K sets the scale and the flow behavior index n sets the curvature: n<1 is shear-thinning, n>1 shear-thickening, n=1 Newtonian.
notes: The units of K depend on n (Pa*s^n), so it is not a plain viscosity. Model has no yield stress; gamma is the shear rate in 1/s.

name: Herschel-Bulkley Shear Stress
description: Combines a yield stress and power-law behavior: the Herschel-Bulkley stress is tau0 + K*gamma^n. The fluid flows only above yield stress tau0, after which stress grows nonlinearly with shear rate gamma governed by K and index n.
notes: Valid only when the material is yielding (stress above tau0). Reduces to Bingham when n=1 and to a power-law fluid when tau0=0; K carries units Pa*s^n.

name: Ergun Equation Pressure Gradient
description: Predicts the pressure drop per unit length for flow through a packed bed of particles. The first term is viscous (Kozeny-Carman-like) and the second is inertial, both scaled strongly by void fraction eps and inversely by particle diameter dp.
notes: eps is the bed void fraction (0-1) and dp the particle diameter; u is the superficial (empty-tube) velocity, not interstitial. Sensitive to eps because of the eps^3 terms.

name: Kozeny-Carman Pressure Gradient
description: Gives the viscous (laminar) pressure gradient for creeping flow through a packed bed, 180*mu*(1-eps)^2*u/(eps^3*dp^2). It is the low-Reynolds limit of the Ergun equation, dominant when inertial effects are negligible.
notes: Valid only for slow (laminar) flow through porous media; at higher velocities add the Ergun inertial term. eps is void fraction and u is superficial velocity.

name: Capillary Length
description: Computes the capillary length sqrt(gamma/(rho*g)), the length scale at which surface tension and gravity balance. Below this scale (a few millimetres for water) surface tension dominates and drops stay nearly spherical.
notes: gamma is surface tension in N/m, rho the liquid density. It sets the size of capillary ripples and the meniscus width; it is a material length, not a droplet size.

name: Galileo Number
description: Returns the Galileo number g*L^3/nu^2, a dimensionless ratio of gravitational to viscous forces using kinematic viscosity nu. It characterizes buoyancy-driven or falling-particle flows without needing a velocity scale.
notes: Dimensionless; nu is kinematic viscosity (m^2/s), L a characteristic length. It is the square of a gravity-based Reynolds number and grows rapidly with L (cube power).

name: Archimedes Number
description: Computes the Archimedes number, the ratio of gravitational buoyancy forces to viscous forces for a particle in a fluid. The driving density difference rhop-rho and particle size L set the tendency to settle or fluidize.
notes: Dimensionless; rhop is particle and rho fluid density, mu dynamic viscosity. A negative value (rhop<rho) means the particle rises rather than settles.

name: Morton Number
description: Gives the Morton number, a fluid property group g*mu^4*(rho-rhog)/(rho^2*sigma^3) that depends only on the liquid, gas, and interface. Together with the Eotvos number it fixes the shape of bubbles or drops rising in a liquid.
notes: Dimensionless and independent of bubble size or velocity. sigma is surface tension; because it appears cubed and mu to the fourth power, small property changes shift it greatly.

name: Weissenberg Number
description: Computes the Weissenberg number lambda*gamma, the product of a fluid's relaxation time lambda and the shear rate gamma. It measures how strongly elastic (viscoelastic) effects appear relative to viscous flow in steady shear.
notes: Dimensionless; gamma is shear rate in 1/s. High values signal strong elastic stresses (rod-climbing, die swell). Distinct from the Deborah number, which uses a flow time scale.

name: Deborah Number
description: Returns the Deborah number lambda/tc, the ratio of a material's relaxation time lambda to the observation (flow) time tc. Small values mean the material acts fluid-like, large values solid-like on the chosen timescale.
notes: Dimensionless; both times in seconds. Note it depends on the observation time tc, so the same material can appear liquid or solid depending on how long you watch it.

name: Taylor Number
description: Computes the Taylor number omega^2*R*d^3/nu^2 for flow between rotating cylinders (Taylor-Couette). It measures centrifugal versus viscous forces and predicts the onset of Taylor vortices when it exceeds a critical value.
notes: Dimensionless; omega is angular velocity, R the mean radius, d the gap, nu kinematic viscosity. Definitions of Ta vary between texts, so compare critical values consistently.

name: Kutta-Joukowski Lift per Span
description: Gives the lift force per unit span on a two-dimensional body from the Kutta-Joukowski theorem: rho*U*Gamma. Lift is proportional to fluid density, freestream speed U, and the circulation Gamma bound to the body.
notes: Result is force per unit span (N/m), not total lift. Valid for inviscid, incompressible 2D flow; Gamma has units m^2/s and its sign sets the lift direction.

name: Blasius Boundary Layer Thickness
description: Estimates the laminar boundary layer thickness on a flat plate as 5*x/sqrt(Rex), where x is distance from the leading edge and Rex the local Reynolds number. The layer grows with the square root of distance.
notes: Valid for laminar flow over a smooth flat plate with zero pressure gradient. Rex must stay below transition (about 5e5); it gives the 99% velocity thickness.

name: Boundary Layer Displacement Thickness
description: Computes the displacement thickness of a laminar flat-plate boundary layer, 1.721*x/sqrt(Rex). It is the distance the outer inviscid flow is pushed away by the slower boundary layer, representing the lost mass flow.
notes: Applies to laminar, zero-pressure-gradient flat-plate flow (Blasius). It is smaller than the 99% thickness and is used to correct effective body shape and inlet areas.

name: Boundary Layer Momentum Thickness
description: Gives the momentum thickness of a laminar flat-plate boundary layer, 0.664*x/sqrt(Rex). It represents the momentum deficit in the boundary layer and is directly related to the wall drag on the plate.
notes: Valid for laminar Blasius flow over a flat plate. It is the smallest of the three thicknesses and links to skin friction via the momentum-integral relation.

name: Laminar Skin Friction Coefficient
description: Returns the local skin friction coefficient 0.664/sqrt(Rex) for laminar flow over a flat plate. It is the dimensionless wall shear stress at distance where the local Reynolds number is Rex.
notes: This is the local (not average) coefficient for laminar Blasius flow; the average over length 0 to x is twice as large. Valid only below transition.

name: Turbulent Boundary Layer Thickness
description: Estimates the turbulent boundary layer thickness on a flat plate as 0.37*x/Rex^0.2, from the one-seventh-power velocity profile. A turbulent layer grows faster with distance than a laminar one.
notes: Valid for a turbulent boundary layer (Rex above about 5e5) on a smooth flat plate with zero pressure gradient; it assumes turbulence starts near the leading edge.

name: Poiseuille Hydraulic Resistance
description: Computes the hydraulic resistance of a circular tube in laminar flow, 8*mu*L/(pi*r^4). It relates pressure drop to flow rate (delta p = R*Q) and rises steeply as the tube radius shrinks (fourth-power dependence).
notes: Valid for steady, fully developed laminar (Poiseuille) flow. The r^4 term makes resistance extremely sensitive to radius; halving r raises resistance sixteenfold.

name: Colebrook Friction Factor (Solved Exactly)
description: Solves the implicit Colebrook–White equation for the Darcy friction factor of turbulent pipe flow (Colebrook 1939), the basis of the Moody chart.
notes: Explicit fits (Swamee–Jain, Haaland) agree within about 1–2 %.

name: Minor Loss Head of a Fitting
description: Gives the head lost in a valve, bend or fitting as K velocity heads (a 90° elbow is about 0.3–0.9, a globe valve about 10).
notes: Add all minor losses to the pipe friction loss.

name: Equivalent Pipe Length of a Fitting
description: Gives the length of straight pipe that causes the same loss as a fitting, so fittings can be added to the pipe length.
notes: A 90° elbow in 50 mm pipe is worth a couple of metres of pipe.

name: Pump Affinity Law: Flow
description: Gives a centrifugal pump's or fan's flow at a new speed: flow is proportional to speed.
notes: Head scales with speed², power with speed³.

name: Pump Affinity Law: Head
description: Gives a pump's head (pressure) at a new speed: head scales with the square of speed.
notes: 80 % speed gives 64 % head.

name: Pump Affinity Law: Power
description: Gives a pump's or fan's power at a new speed: power scales with the cube of speed — why variable-speed drives save so much energy.
notes: 80 % speed needs only about 51 % power.

name: Pump Specific Speed
description: Classifies a pump by shape: low values are radial (centrifugal), high values mixed and axial flow.
notes: In these SI units, about 10–35 radial, 35–160 mixed, above 160 axial.

name: Net Positive Suction Head Available

variables.label: Liquid level above pump inlet (negative if below)

description: Gives the NPSH available at a pump inlet; it must exceed the pump's NPSH required or the pump cavitates.
notes: Hot water (higher vapour pressure) sharply lowers NPSH available.

name: Pump Shaft Power
description: Gives the power the motor must deliver to the pump shaft: hydraulic power divided by pump efficiency.
notes: Divide again by motor efficiency for the electrical input.

name: Stokes Number
description: Compares a particle's response time with the flow's: above 1 particles leave the streamlines and hit obstacles.
notes: Governs dust filters, inhalers and spray drying.

name: Fraction of a Floating Body Submerged
description: Gives the share of a floating object's volume below the surface: the density ratio (Archimedes).
notes: About 89 % of an iceberg in seawater is hidden.

name: Time to Drain a Tank through an Orifice
description: Gives the time to empty a straight-sided tank through a hole in the bottom, integrating Torricelli's law.
notes: Time is proportional to √h, so the top half of the depth drains faster than the bottom half.

name: Sluice Gate Discharge
expression: cd * b * a * sqrt(2 * g * h)
description: Gives the flow under a sluice gate from its opening, width and the upstream water depth.
notes: Cd is typically 0.55–0.61 for free flow.

name: Broad-Crested Weir Discharge
description: Gives the flow over a broad-crested weir, where the water passes critical depth on the crest (1.705 = (2/3)^1.5·√g).
notes: Used for measuring flow in rivers and canals.

name: Pressure inside a Soap Bubble
description: Gives the excess pressure in a soap bubble, which has two surfaces: 4σ/R (a droplet has one: 2σ/R).
notes: Smaller bubbles have higher pressure, so connected bubbles empty the small into the large.

name: Area–Mach Relation (A/A*)
description: Gives the nozzle area needed at Mach M relative to the throat area where Mach 1 is reached.
notes: Mach 2 needs 1.6875 times the throat area — the basis of rocket-nozzle design.

name: Choked Mass Flow through a Nozzle
description: Gives the maximum mass flow through a nozzle or orifice once the flow at the throat reaches Mach 1; lowering the downstream pressure further does not increase it.
notes: Used to size relief valves and gas orifices.
